summary: This experimental RFC specifies a common interface for using the Host Identity Protocol (HIP) with a Distributed Hash Table service. It provides lookups from name to Host Identity Tag, and from Host Identity Tag to address.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a phone book shared by many computers. You ask it for a name and it gives you an identity tag, and you can then ask it where that tag currently lives.

questions: what is the host identity protocol
what is a distributed hash table
subtitle: Using distributed hash tables to look up Host Identity Protocol addresses

tldr.problem: The Host Identity Protocol uses cryptographic identifiers (HITs) instead of IP addresses, but there's no standard way to discover where a HIT is currently located on the Internet. DNS works well for domain names, but HITs are not tied to the hierarchical DNS namespace.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a standard way to use a Distributed Hash Table (DHT) as a lookup service: one service maps human-readable names to HITs, and another maps HITs to current IP addresses. Both services publish and retrieve data in a common HIP resource record format.
tldr.outcome: HIP deployments can now use a shared DHT infrastructure for peer discovery. Applications can look up where to reach a specific HIT without pre-configuration, making HIP more practical. The approach is experimental and works alongside existing alternatives like DNS.

today: RFC 6537 remains Experimental. The OpenDHT service it references was retired in 2009. However, the standardized interface continues to be compatible with alternative DHT implementations. Most HIP deployments today use DNS or static pre-configuration for peer discovery rather than DHT, but the RFC provides a foundation for any implementation that wants to use distributed lookup services.

sections.title: The HIP Discovery Problem
sections.content:
The Host Identity Protocol (HIP) replaces IP addresses as the primary identifier with public-key-based Host Identity Tags (HITs). This has security benefits, but it breaks the one assumption that DNS has always made: that hierarchical names map to addresses. In HIP, the identifier (HIT) is a hash of the public key itself. It is not hierarchical, not human-friendly, and not tied to the domain system.

This RFC addresses the problem by standardizing how HIP implementations can use a Distributed Hash Table (DHT)—a peer-to-peer database spread across the Internet—to discover HITs and their current locations. DHTs are good at this job: they can store arbitrary data, scale to many servers, and handle updates more frequently than the hierarchical DNS system.
sections.plainLanguage: HIP uses security ID codes instead of IP addresses, but nobody can find where those codes live. This RFC lets computers use a shared notebook (a DHT) to look things up.

sections.title: The OpenDHT Interface
sections.content:
The RFC standardizes around the OpenDHT service, which was a free public DHT deployed on about 150 PlanetLab nodes. OpenDHT provided three operations: put (store a value by a key), get (retrieve values by key), and rm (remove). Keys are limited to 20 bytes, values to 1024 bytes, and each entry has a time-to-live (TTL) in seconds, up to one week.

For HIP use, the RFC defines a common data format called the HIP DHT Resource Record (HDRR). The HDRR is encoded like a HIP packet—using TLV (type-length-value) parameters—even though it is stored in the DHT, not sent on the wire. This reuses HIP's encoding, making implementation straightforward for HIP developers.
sections.plainLanguage: The OpenDHT was a notebook service run by computers on the Internet. You could store something and give everyone the page number; later, you could tell it a page number and get your data back.

sections.title: Name-to-HIT and Address Lookups
sections.content:
The RFC defines two independent lookup services. The name-to-HIT lookup takes a human-readable name (a hostname, FQDN, or any alias), hashes it with SHA-1 to fit the DHT's 20-byte key limit, and retrieves the corresponding HIT. An optional X.509 certificate can be included to prove that someone is authorized to use that name. This service helps when DNS does not support HIP resource records or a host has no DNS authority.

The address lookup takes a HIT as input and returns the host's current IP address (locators), along with validation data. The HIT is truncated to avoid uneven distribution in the DHT (the common ORCHID prefix is dropped), and the address record includes a signature and sequence number so clients can verify freshness and authenticity. This is essential because HIP hosts are mobile: addresses change when a host moves, but its HIT remains the same.
sections.plainLanguage: One service lets you ask 'What is Alice's HIT?' and it gives you a 128-bit number. Another service lets you ask 'Where is this HIT right now?' and it gives you an IP address and proves it's the real answer.

sections.title: HIP DHT Resource Record Structure
sections.content:
Both lookups use the HDRR format. For a name-to-HIT record, the HDRR contains only the HIT (in the Sender's HIT field) and optionally a certificate. For an address-lookup record, it contains locators (IP addresses), a sequence number for ordering multiple records, the host's public-key identity, an optional certificate, and a digital signature over the whole record.

The sequence number is important because the DHT does not replace old values; if a host publishes a new address without removing the old one first, both exist in the DHT. A client performing a lookup retrieves all records and picks the one with the highest sequence number to find the most recent address.
sections.plainLanguage: The data format is a small HIP packet that contains either just a name and its identity code, or an identity code, its current addresses, and a signature proving it is real.

sections.title: Security and Limitations
sections.content:
The name-to-HIT lookup has no inherent security: anyone can publish a HIT for any name. Certificates can help, but only if the client trusts the certificate authority. The address lookup is more secure because each record is signed by the holder of the HIT. A client can verify the signature using the public-key identity contained in the record. However, unless the DHT server itself validates signatures (which requires modifications to OpenDHT), an attacker can still pollute the DHT by replaying old signed records with the same or a higher sequence number.

Clients should always validate records retrieved from an untrusted DHT server. The RFC also notes that private addresses (like 192.168.1.0/24) should not be published; for hosts behind NAT, the address of a Rendezvous Server can be published instead. The 1024-byte limit on DHT values constrains the size of Host Identities and certificates that can be stored.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone can claim to be Alice in the name lookup. For addresses, there is a signature that proves a record is real, but a bad actor can still keep old records alive unless the DHT server checks signatures.

sections.title: Practical Use and Current Status
sections.content:
The RFC recommends that hosts publish their HIT when they start up and refresh it before its TTL expires. They should also publish address updates whenever their preferred address changes. Clients can use the name-to-HIT service to discover peers without pre-configuration, and the address lookup to get current locators before or during a HIP association.

The OpenDHT service that the RFC is based on was retired in 2009. Alternative implementations like OpenLookup and open-source Bamboo DHT deployments remain compatible with the interface. The RFC remains Experimental because DHT-based HIP discovery has not seen widespread deployment; DNS and pre-configuration remain the dominant discovery methods for HIP. However, the standardized interface provides a foundation for any HIP deployment that wants to use DHT infrastructure.
sections.plainLanguage: When a computer starts up, it puts its HIT and address in the shared notebook. Other computers can look them up anytime. The original notebook service closed, but the interface still works with other DHT services.
